column1: The engine is uncertain about DA prices, intraday prices, imbalance prices, aFRR capacity clearing prices, aFRR activation volumes and direction, site load, and PV simultaneously.
Valuation needs distributions rather than point forecasts, because PeakView uses a CVaR tail, AfrrCapacity needs an expected bid-curve value, and ImbalanceRisk is by definition a tail quantity.
The entire cross-market problem is driven by correlation.
aFRR activation is correlated with imbalance prices, which are correlated with intraday prices, which are correlated with the residual load that also drives the site's own load and PV.
A high-price hour is precisely the hour where the peak charge bites, the aFRR is activated, and the battery is wanted in three places at once.
Sampling each series from its own marginal destroys exactly the dependence structure that determines whether the co-optimisation is worth anything.
Per-series marginal sampling systematically overstates the value of the strategy, because it lets the engine believe it can be lucky in one market and unlucky in another independently.
There is one joint ensemble with one scenario axis, shared by every uncertain series.
The ensemble has shape [S scenarios] × [H slots] × [K series], stored as float32 struct-of-arrays by series, with weights of shape [S] that are non-negative and sum to 1.
K is the number of series, S_gen the number of generated scenarios, and S the number of reduced scenarios that reach the Planner, which is C1's scenarioCount.
Scenario reduction maps S_gen to S with S much smaller than S_gen.
Scenario s is a coherent state of the world, so price[s,t], load[s,t], pv[s,t] and activation[s,t] all belong to the same draw.
Any code that indexes one series by s and another by s' is a defect.
Scenario weights are explicit and generally non-uniform, because the ensemble that reaches the Planner is a reduced one.
Scenario reduction by fast-forward selection or Wasserstein-optimal reduction maps the generated ensemble to S representatives with weights.
The scenario reduction is a materialised artefact, reproducible and versioned.
The ensemble is generated in one place, from a joint model, offline, and its output is the artefact.
The engine consumes scenarios and never assembles them from marginals.
Exactly two derived forms may cross C1 — QuantileView and TailStatistic — both computed from the joint ensemble and never independently.
QuantileView carries marginal quantiles for views that genuinely need only a marginal.
TailStatistic carries CVaR-type functionals computed as a weighted empirical mean over the joint ensemble, and is what PeakView uses.
Ensemble memory is S × H × K × 4 bytes, which for K=8, H=192 and S=64 is about 400 kB per snapshot.
The scenario axis is affordable because the hot window is bounded.
Scenario count S is a first-class tuning parameter with a measurable cost/quality curve.
T5 requires reporting objective value and solve time as a function of S, so the choice of S is evidenced rather than guessed.
The Planner's stochastic formulations — chance constraints, CVaR, two-stage recourse — all index the same scenario axis, so they are mutually consistent by construction.
Any single-series forecast improvement must be re-integrated into the joint model rather than patched in downstream.
Re-integrating single-series improvements into the joint model is a real workflow cost and is the price of correctness.
The reduced ensemble preserves the mean of each marginal within tolerance.
Independent per-series distributions destroy dependence and bias the strategy's apparent value upward.
A point forecast plus a risk add-on cannot express tail co-movement, which is where the imbalance and peak risk live.
Solve time scales with S, so reduction with weights gives most of the accuracy at a fraction of the cost, and the loss is measurable against a large-S reference run.

The five-layer pipeline is intended to be one-directional, and two dependencies break that: λ_SOC being a dual of the Planner's optimisation, and peak_to_go and the §19(2) qualification state depending on realised history.

There is a third feedback dependency, the commitment ledger: orders filled at the DA gate constrain the intraday solve and aFRR capacity awarded constrains the SOC corridor for the whole delivery block.
If the feedback dependencies are handled ad hoc, the architecture's central claim of one-directional, independently testable seams becomes false, and nothing downstream of that claim holds either.
L0, the State/Value Store, is the only backwards path and is always read at a lag of at least one tick.
L0 holds exactly the state that must survive a tick.
The realised POI peak per accounting period and per tariff window is written by L5, read by L2's PeakView, on the C_accounting clock.
The §19(2) qualification state — accumulated energy, full-load hours, HLZF exposure — is written by L5, read by L2's TariffView, on the C_accounting clock.
The commitment ledger of awarded aFRR blocks, filled spot positions and open orders is written by L5 when confirmed and by L3 when pending, read by L3, on the C_gate clock.
The value function V(SOC, peakState, qualState) is written by the slow loop, read by L2 and then L3, on the C_slow clock.
The data quality state and degradation mode are written by L1 and L5, read by all layers, on the C_tick clock.
The model artefact versions in force are written by the manifest, read by all layers, once per run.
L0 is snapshotted at the top of the tick into an immutable StateSnapshot and written only at the end of the tick from L5's output.
The commitment ledger distinguishes pending entries, where the Planner submitted intent, from confirmed entries, where Execution reported a fill or award.
The Planner treats pending commitments as probabilistic exposure and confirmed commitments as hard constraints.
The pending/confirmed distinction is what makes the continuous intraday loop safe, letting it re-optimise around orders that may or may not fill without either double-selling or double-counting.
The dependency graph is a DAG within a tick and can be verified mechanically.
T3 includes an acyclicity audit that instruments each layer's reads and writes during a replay and asserts no read of a same-tick write.
The StateSnapshot is a contract, C5's mirror image, with a field table, a version and invariants like every other seam.
Lag is explicit and therefore priceable: the Planner knows the peak state is as of the last settled interval and can be conservative about the unsettled gap rather than pretending it is current.
Restart and warm-start are straightforward because L0 is the entire state: an engine restart loads a StateSnapshot and continues.
L0 must be durably persisted with the same content-addressing as everything else.
L0 costs an extra component and the discipline of routing everything through it even when a direct reference would be shorter.
Letting Valuation call the Planner to get λ is circular and untestable, and the Planner's problem is not well posed without the valuation it would be computing.
For fixed-point iteration within a tick, convergence is not guaranteed, solve time becomes unbounded, and the result is not reproducible under a time limit.
A global mutable service works until two components read it at different points in the tick and get different answers, at which point nothing is reproducible.
λ_SOC is the number that makes cheap MWh now versus expensive MWh later tradeable.
A scalar λ_SOC is a linearisation around an assumed operating point.

The true marginal value of stored energy depends on how much is stored: near-empty energy is worth much more than near-full energy when a peak event is possible, and much less when the next opportunity is a cheap charging window.
A single λ prices only one point on the marginal-value curve and misprices every other point.
The mispricing from a scalar λ is quantitatively serious in a BTM setting.

The peak charge creates a large, state-dependent kink: the marginal value of the kWh that keeps the site below the peak threshold is enormous while the marginal value of the next one is close to the spot spread.
No scalar represents both sides of the peak-threshold kink.
The horizon is closed by a value function published as a concave piecewise-linear curve.
V maps SOC to EUR, published as breakpoints {(e_i, v_i)} for i = 0..n with strictly decreasing slopes, conditioned on peakState, qualState and calendar context.
The Planner adds V(soc[T_end]) to its objective as a maximisation term.
Because V is concave and the objective is a maximisation, the PWL requires no binary variables and is representable with a λ-formulation or as the minimum of its affine pieces.
The LP relaxation of the concave terminal-value PWL is exact.
Exactness of the LP relaxation is the property that makes the value function affordable.
λ_SOC is the subgradient of V at the optimal terminal SOC and the Planner can report it for diagnostics.
λ_SOC is an output and not an input, which inverts the original dependency and removes the cycle.
V is produced by the slow loop as a rolling-horizon or approximate dynamic programming solve over a horizon long enough to see the end of the accounting period, using the joint ensemble.
V is written to L0 and read by L2 and L3 at a lag.
Concavity of V is enforced rather than assumed: the fitting step projects onto the concave hull and the contract validates strictly decreasing slopes.
The underlying value can be genuinely non-concave around a §19(2) qualification cliff.
Genuine non-concavity is not smoothed away silently but represented explicitly as a separate discrete state dimension, with a concave V conditional on each state.
V is concave in SOC given the discrete state, and discreteness is handled by the discrete state.
The terminal-value problem, the main source of myopia in rolling optimisation, is solved properly rather than by a hand-tuned end-of-horizon SOC target.
The Planner's horizon can be shortened, a real solve-time saving, because the truncation is priced rather than ignored.
V is a first-class artefact: versioned, content-hashed, replayable, and independently testable against realised P&L.
A better V improves every decision downstream, so the slow loop is where research effort compounds.
Staleness of V must be handled, and the degradation ladder defines behaviour when V is older than its validity window.
A scalar λ from Valuation is circular and a poor approximation at exactly the states that matter.
A fixed terminal SOC target wastes value whenever the target is wrong, and the target is always wrong.
Using a long horizon instead of a value function makes solve time grow, forecast quality collapses beyond a few days, and the accounting period boundary can be a month away.
A convex quadratic approximation of V is cheaper to fit but cannot represent the peak-threshold kink, which is the most important feature of the curve.
